Wave equation (utt​=c2Δu)

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Analysis Partial differential equation
OurBigBook.com Words: 17k Articles: 213
The wave equation is a second-order linear partial differential equation describing waves with finite propagation speed. In one spatial dimension its homogeneous, constant-coefficient form is
utt​=c2uxx​,c>0.
(1)
Here x is position, t is time, u(x,t) is the disturbance, and subscripts denote partial derivatives. For a wave equation on a string, u is transverse displacement; in linear acoustics, it can be a pressure perturbation. In several spatial dimensions, uxx​ becomes the Laplacian Δu. The same mathematical structure connects vibrating strings and acoustic waves, although their physical assumptions and wave speeds differ. [ref]
For the whole-line Cauchy problem, prescribe both displacement u(x,0)=f(x) and velocity ut​(x,0)=g(x). A classical solution has continuous partial derivatives through order two; f∈C2(R) and g∈C1(R) suffice for D'Alembert's formula to produce one. A finite string additionally needs boundary conditions. These statements concern the unforced model with constant c; damping, spatially varying coefficients and nonlinear terms change the solution formula.
A travelling wave F(x−ct) carries its entire profile to the right at wave speed c; G(x+ct) travels left. Their sum is again a solution by the superposition principle. A standing wave instead has a fixed mode shape whose size and sign oscillate: in sin(kx)cos(ckt), each node of a standing wave stays stationary. The distinction is especially clear in the pulse and string diagrams below. For this ideal model, the dispersion relation is ω2=c2k2: each propagation branch is nondispersive, so a localized profile translates without spreading. This makes the equation a useful reference against which to understand wave dispersion and damping.
The appealing combination is local interaction with global predictability: neighbouring displacements determine acceleration through uxx​, yet D'Alembert's formula explicitly identifies exactly which initial locations can influence a later observation. Finite propagation speed turns that observation into a domain of dependence, rather than requiring knowledge of the entire initial string.

Regular time-harmonic spherical wave (u(r,t)=Asin(ωt)sin(ωr/c)/(ωr/c))

Words: 74
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
For a spherically symmetric function, v=ru reduces the radial wave equation to vtt​=c2vrr​. A time-harmonic separated solution has radial numerator Csin(kr)+Dcos(kr), with k=ω/c. Finiteness at the origin excludes D, and the prescribed finite origin value fixes C. This is a standing combination of incoming and outgoing waves. A purely outgoing point-source wave instead has a 1/r singularity and must be specified by its source strength, not by a finite value at the origin.

All-time boundedness of a wave equation with a reaction term (α<λ1​)

Words: 73
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
For utt​=Δu+αu with a homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition, let λ1​>0 be the first Dirichlet Laplacian eigenvalue. On a bounded one-dimensional interval, finite-energy displacement remains bounded for all time and all initial data exactly when α<λ1​. The conserved energy 21​(∥ut​∥22​+∥∇u∥22​−α∥u∥22​) controls the gradient and, by the Poincaré inequality and one-dimensional integration, the maximum norm. At equality a mode can grow linearly; above it a mode can grow exponentially. Bounded oscillations need not have a long-time limit.

Vector field method for wave equations

Words: 254 Articles: 7
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
The vector field method commutes a wave equation with spacetime symmetry generators, estimates the resulting commuted wave energies, and converts weighted L2 norms to pointwise decay using a Klainerman-Sobolev inequality. The commutation vector fields for the wave equation include translations, rotations, Lorentz boost vector fields and the scaling vector field. It is useful for almost global existence for wave equations and for small-data global existence under the classical null condition for wave equations.

The wave energy estimate controls its growth through commuted sources, while the Klainerman-Sobolev inequality gives pointwise decay for low-order derivatives.

Klainerman-Sobolev inequality (∣u∣≲(1+t+r)(1+∣t−r∣)1/2∑∣I∣≤2​∥ZIu∥2​​)

Vector field method for wave equations OurBigBook.com

This weighted Sobolev inequality converts control of commuted wave energy into decay. It holds independently of any wave equation satisfied by u.

Commutation vector field for the wave equation

Words: 137 Articles: 4
Vector field method for wave equations OurBigBook.com
A first-order vector field Z is a commutation field for the flat wave equation when [□,Z] is zero or a controlled multiple of □. Translations, spatial rotations and Lorentz boost vector fields commute with □; the scaling vector field satisfies [□,S]=2□. Repeated commutation preserves the differential order of a semilinear wave equation.

Scaling vector field (S=t∂t​+x⋅∇)

Commutation vector field for the wave equation OurBigBook.com
The vector field S=t∂t​+x⋅∇ generates simultaneous spacetime dilation. For the flat d'Alembert operator, [□,S]=2□. Consequently it commutes with the homogeneous wave equation at the level of its solution set, although its operator commutator is nonzero.

Reflected-step solution of the wave equation (y(x,t))

Words: 78
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
For ytt​=c2yxx​ on 0<x<L, initially at rest with zero displacement, apply y(0,t)=a for t>0 and keep y(L,t)=0. A geometric series in the Laplace transform gives
y(x,t)=a∑m≥0​[H(t−c2mL+x​)−H(t−c(2m+2)L−x​)].
(2)
Here H is the Heaviside step function, L,c>0, and only finitely many terms contribute at any finite time. The second step in each pair is a sign-reversed reflection from the fixed endpoint. The formula solves the wave equation classically away from the fronts and distributionally across them; the midpoint is a square wave of period 2L/c.

Wave speed (c)

Words: 527 Articles: 5
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
For the homogeneous one-dimensional wave equation utt​=c2uxx​ with constant c>0, wave speed means the speed at which a travelling wave profile translates. In F(x−ct), a feature initially at x=s follows x=s+ct, giving signed velocity +c; in G(x+ct) it follows x=s−ct, giving signed velocity −c. The characteristic lines for the one-dimensional wave equation therefore have slopes dx/dt=±c. The speed of either profile is c, even though the displacement at a fixed point can change sign or pass through zero.[ref]
The same c bounds the causal cone for the constant-speed wave equation. For a wave equation on a string, c=T/μ​ depends on tension and linear mass density; for small acoustic waves in stationary uniform air it is the speed of sound. This interpretation assumes the stated ideal wave equation. In media with wave dispersion, phase velocity, group velocity and the earliest signal arrival have different meanings: a measured wave crest speed need not be the speed of a wave envelope, and neither alone establishes a causal cone for the constant-speed wave equation.

Acoustic time-of-flight speed measurement (c=d/Δt)

Words: 360 Articles: 3
Wave speed OurBigBook.com
The experiment in A time of flight method to measure the speed of sound using a stereo sound card by Carlos C. Carvalho and others makes wave speed visible as a delay. Two powered microphones feed separate channels of one stereo line input. A clap beyond one end of their common axis reaches the nearer microphone first. The displayed signals show two separated onsets when enlarged; count their sample separation N to obtain Δt=N/fs​ and infer speed of sound c=d/Δt from the measured microphone spacing d. The reported sampling rate is 44100s−1. Repeating at different spacings gives a distance-versus-delay plot whose slope estimates speed of sound; dependence on distance helps identify acoustic travel rather than a fixed electronic delay. These are the paper's apparatus and observed readout, not measurements made for this article.[ref]
A controlled implementation also needs timing calibration for acoustic speed measurements. Put the microphones side by side to estimate the channel-delay offset τ0​, swap channels to check its sign, and check the acquisition clock against an independent timing reference. Measure spacings between consistent points on the microphones, keep the source outside their span and on their axis, and fit Δt=d/c+τ0​ by linear regression rather than forcing a zero intercept. Repeat pulses and compare the same onset criterion before reflections arrive. These are proposed calibration and control checks, not additional procedures claimed for the paper.
One sample corresponds to 1/fs​≃22.7μs for the reported sampling rate, so a delay of only a few samples has large relative measurement error. Background measurement noise, different microphone responses and threshold choice can move the apparent onset; reflections can supply a later competing pulse. Record temperature, keep air motion small, and compare several spacings. The result estimates speed of sound under those conditions; it cannot prove an exactly zero precursor below the instrument's sensitivity or establish finite propagation speed for every real medium. Both new diagrams in these sections show explicitly synthetic ideal wave equation solutions.[ref]

A constant offset changes the intercept of a delay-versus-distance linear regression; a clock-scale error changes the inferred speed of sound itself.

Slowness is the reciprocal of phase velocity, measured in time per distance. A plane wave with wavevector k and angular frequency ω has vector slowness p=k/ω. Its direction is the wavefront normal, which need not be the group velocity direction in an anisotropic medium.

Method of descent for the wave equation

Words: 50
Kirchhoff formula OurBigBook.com
Extend lower-dimensional data independently of an extra coordinate and apply the higher-dimensional wave equation solution. Projecting a three-dimensional sphere to the planar disk yields the kernel [2πt2−r2​]−1 for the two-dimensional solution with zero initial displacement. This method of descent for the wave equation explains why three-dimensional wave propagation can depend on a sphere while two-dimensional propagation depends on its interior.

Strong Huygens principle

Words: 37
Kirchhoff formula OurBigBook.com
The strong Huygens principle says that the three-dimensional wave solution at (t,x) depends only on initial data on the sphere ∣y−x∣=∣t∣. A compactly supported disturbance therefore leaves no tail in the interior of its light cone.

Finite propagation speed

Words: 472 Articles: 5
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
For the unforced, constant-c one-dimensional wave equation, finite propagation speed says that changing Cauchy data outside [x∗​−ct∗​,x∗​+ct∗​] cannot change the solution at (x∗​,t∗​), where c>0 and t∗​≥0. This interval is the initial-data domain of dependence. Its endpoints are found by following the two characteristic lines for the one-dimensional wave equation backwards from the observation. D'Alembert's formula makes the dependence sharper: initial displacement is sampled at the endpoints, while initial velocity is integrated over the entire interval.[ref]
For the synthetic choice c=1, (x∗​,t∗​)=(0.5,1.5) has initial-data domain of dependence [−1,2]. A change confined near x=3 is irrelevant to that observation, however large it is. If both Cauchy data vanish outside [−a,a], their compact support can influence only [−a−ct,a+ct] at t≥0. Thus an observer at x>a sees exactly zero displacement for 0≤t<(x−a)/c. There is no nonzero precursor beyond this causal cone for the constant-speed wave equation in the ideal model. This is an exact statement about the partial differential equation, stronger than an experimental failure to detect a small signal.
Support widening for the wave equation is a bound on possible influence, not a claim that every point inside the expanding interval moves. A bump function released with zero initial velocity splits into two separated travelling waves; the middle can become empty. An initial kick can instead leave an interior tail, as in the D'Alembert formula with initial velocity. Consequently finite propagation speed does not imply the Strong Huygens principle. A finite string needs boundary conditions, and the whole-line formula applies locally only until its backward causal cone for the constant-speed wave equation encounters an endpoint.

Causal cone for the constant-speed wave equation (∣x−x∗​∣≤c(t∗​−t))

Words: 64
Finite propagation speed OurBigBook.com
For c>0, the backward causal cone at (x∗​,t∗​) is
Cc−​(x∗​,t∗​)={(x,t):0≤t≤t∗​, ∣x−x∗​∣≤c(t∗​−t)}.
(4)
Its boundaries are characteristic lines for the one-dimensional wave equation; its base on t=0 is the initial-data domain of dependence. The forward cone from (s,0) is t≥0, ∣x−s∣≤ct. Here the cone is set by the model's wave speed, which may be acoustic or a string wave speed; it does not assert propagation at the speed of light.

Support widening for the wave equation (suppu(⋅,t)⊆[−a−ct,a+ct])

Words: 63
Finite propagation speed OurBigBook.com
For whole-line Cauchy data with support contained in [−a,a], the displayed inclusion holds at t≥0. A short check uses D'Alembert's formula: if x>a+ct, both sampled endpoints and the whole interval of integration lie to the right of a, so all contributions vanish; the argument for x<−a−ct is identical. The inclusion can be strict, and a nonzero response at the first permitted arrival is not guaranteed.

Weak Huygens principle

Words: 51
Finite propagation speed OurBigBook.com
The weak Huygens principle is the domain-of-dependence statement that initial data outside a backward light cone cannot influence its tip. It permits an interior tail and is weaker than the Strong Huygens principle. For utt​−Δu+V(x)u=0 with V≥0, integrating the local energy over shrinking balls proves this statement: the boundary contribution is ut​∂ν​u−21​(ut2​+∣∇u∣2+Vu2)≤0.

Shrinking cone energy argument

Words: 42

Damping

Words: 2k Articles: 11
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
Damping dissipates the energy of an oscillation, reducing its amplitude. A linearly damped string applies this mechanism to each normal mode.
Why can stronger damping make a return to equilibrium slower? A weak brake lets a spring exchange potential energy with kinetic energy many times; a very strong brake makes the final motion creep. Critical damping marks the boundary between these behaviours. The distinction depends on the force law: the classification below concerns a single damped harmonic oscillator with viscous damping, rather than every mechanism that removes energy.
Let x(t) be displacement from equilibrium, m>0 the moving mass, k>0 the spring constant, and b≥0 the constant coefficient of viscous damping. With no driving force, Newton's second law gives
mx¨+bx˙+kx=0,x(0)=x0​,x˙(0)=v0​.
(19)
The two initial conditions specify displacement and velocity. Define the undamped eigenfrequency as an angular frequency ω0​=k/m​ and the damping ratio as ζ=b/(2mk​). The ordinary differential equation becomes x¨+2ζω0​x˙+ω02​x=0. A constant weight in a vertical spring merely shifts equilibrium; it is already absorbed in the definition of x.[ref]
For example, the ideal parameters m=1kg and k=4Nm−1 give ω0​=2s−1 and critical damping at b=4kgs−1. Values b=1,4,8kgs−1 give damping ratios 0.25,1,2, respectively. These are model choices, not measured values. For release from rest with x0​>0, set X=x/x0​ and τ=ω0​t; then X′′+2ζX′+X=0, where primes now denote derivatives with respect to τ.
The left panel uses identical initial conditions X(0)=1, X′(0)=0. Underdamping produces repeated crossings of equilibrium; critical damping and overdamping give positive decreasing responses. The right panel keeps critical damping but changes initial velocity: X′(0)=−2 gives one crossing, although there is no oscillation. Both panels are exact model predictions.

Critical damping (ζ=1,bcrit​=2mk​)

Words: 259
Damping OurBigBook.com
Critical damping is the repeated-root case of the viscous damping model: its two characteristic roots coincide at r=−ω0​. The solution with arbitrary initial conditions is
x(t)=[x0​+(v0​+ω0​x0​)t]e−ω0​t.
(20)
The extra factor t is essential: one exponential function alone cannot fit arbitrary initial displacement and velocity when the characteristic equation has a double polynomial root. Substitution, or taking the limit of the underdamped formula as its angular frequency tends to zero, gives the displayed expression.
The precise fastest-return statement is this: hold m, k, x0​>0 and v0​=0 fixed, and compare all ζ≥1. Every response decreases positively toward equilibrium; the critically damped response
xc​(t)=x0​(1+ω0​t)e−ω0​t
(21)
is smaller than every overdamped response at each t>0. It therefore reaches and stays within any specified band ∣x∣≤ϵx0​, 0<ϵ<1, sooner than those responses. Exact arrival at rest takes infinite time. This is a comparison among nonoscillatory regimes for these particular initial conditions, not a universal minimum of every possible settling-time criterion.
One short comparison argument uses q=∂X/∂ζ. Its initial conditions are zero and q′′+2ζq′+q=−2X′. For release from rest, X′<0 at τ>0; the causal Green function of a damped oscillator is positive at positive time for ζ≥1. Its convolution with −2X′ gives q>0: increasing damping beyond the critical value increases the remaining displacement.
There is no repeated oscillation at critical damping, but there can be overshoot once. For x0​>0, the factor in square brackets crosses zero precisely when v0​<−ω0​x0​, at
t∗​=−v0​+ω0​x0​x0​​>0.
(22)
For example, v0​=−2ω0​x0​ gives x=x0​(1−ω0​t)e−ω0​t, crossing equilibrium at t=1/ω0​ as shown above. An overdamped response can also cross once for suitable initial conditions. Conversely, specially chosen initial conditions can remove its slow exponential decay entirely. Thus the generic slow-root argument must not be applied to a response whose slow-root coefficient is zero.

Words: 312 Articles: 2

Viscous damping means a force proportional to, and opposite to, velocity: Fd​=−bx˙ with b≥0. Its coefficient has units kgs−1, equivalently Nsm−1. The name describes a force law; eddy-current damping can approximate the same law without a viscous fluid. Constant m, b and k produce a linear ordinary differential equation, allowing superposition of responses. Kinetic friction with approximately constant magnitude and quadratic drag obey different laws, so their decay need not have the exponential decay or critical threshold derived here.

The damping ratio is the dimensionless ratio b/bcrit​. Substituting the exponential function x=ert into the viscous damping model gives the characteristic equation and its characteristic roots:

(23)
For 0<ζ<1, underdamping gives a pair of complex conjugate roots with negative real part. For ζ=1, critical damping gives the repeated negative real root. For ζ>1, overdamping gives two distinct negative real roots. At ζ=0 the roots are purely imaginary and the harmonic oscillator is undamped; this boundary case has no energy loss. With m,k>0, negative b would inject energy and lies outside the dissipative model.
The left panel locates r/ω0​ in the complex plane; the imaginary part gives the damped angular frequency, while the negative real part gives the exponential decay rate. The right panel shows the positive rates −Re(r±​)/ω0​. Beyond critical damping, one root moves toward zero, explaining slow late motion for generic initial conditions. The repeated-root solution also has a polynomial prefactor, so these rates alone do not describe its complete response.

Damping measurement from free decay

Words: 612 Articles: 3
Damping OurBigBook.com
An experimentally useful question is whether the disappearing oscillation follows viscous damping, and whether increasing the brake changes b rather than m or k. A published teaching protocol uses a cart on an air track, attached between two springs, with ceramic magnets providing eddy-current damping and an ultrasonic motion sensor recording position against time. Replace the magnets with equal masses in the baseline trial so the moving mass stays fixed. Obtain each spring constant from the slope of applied force versus extension, then use k=k1​+k2​. Time many baseline cycles to check ω0​≃k/m​. Compare one-magnet and two-magnet free decays; the protocol calls for a fit of the full trace including its offset. [ref]
The following additional controls make the inference testable. Level the air track and hold its air supply fixed. Check the ultrasonic motion sensor at several stationary flag positions against a ruler, including the full planned travel range; record the offset and scale correction. Check elapsed acquisition time against an independent clock, and choose a sampling rate that resolves many samples within the shortest expected oscillation period. Record the resting equilibrium before and after each run. Release the cart from a small measured displacement with minimal initial velocity, with the driving apparatus inactive. Repeat at several release sizes and magnet settings while keeping the springs and total mass unchanged. These are proposed calibration and repeatability checks, not reported measurements from the source.
For underdamping, fit the recorded position to y(t)=yeq​+Ae−αtcos(ωd​t+ϕ) by nonlinear regression. The readout to inspect is a sequence of alternating extrema about yeq​ with shrinking amplitudes, and the deviations of the fitted curve from the recorded points. The model predicts
α=2mb​=ζω0​,α2+ωd2​=mk​.
(27)
Compare the right-hand side, determined independently from mass and spring constants, with the fitted left-hand side. A good fit supports a constant-coefficient single normal mode over the observed range; it does not establish a universal microscopic force law. The published protocol denotes the decay rate by b and the velocity-proportional coefficient by c; here they are α and b, respectively.
At critical damping or overdamping, fit the corresponding nonoscillatory response including its offset and both initial conditions, rather than forcing a damped cosine onto the data. Adjusting the brake can explore the transition, but the cited protocol does not establish that its one-magnet or two-magnet settings attain critical damping. A near-critical trace over a short interval can be hard to distinguish from neighbouring damping ratios.
Important limitations are finite sensor range, missed or reflected acoustic wave pulses, measurement noise near equilibrium, nonzero release velocity, and position-dependent magnetic braking. Changing the release size tests for quadratic drag or nonlinear spring response; inspecting deviations near turning points can expose kinetic friction. Slow drift of the offset can imitate a long overdamped tail. Report uncertainties in fitted rates and independently measured m,k; absence of a visible crossing only bounds the behaviour within the instrument's sensitivity and recording interval. No numerical experimental results are asserted here.

Normal mode

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
A normal mode, also called an eigenmode, is a pattern of free oscillation in a linear system whose relative displacements stay fixed while a single temporal factor changes their size and sign. For an undamped stable vibrational mode,
u(x,t)=ϕ(x)q(t),q(t)=Acos(ωt+φ).
(37)
Here ϕ is the mode shape, A sets the amplitude, ω is the eigenfrequency expressed as an angular frequency, and φ is the oscillation phase. Every snapshot is a scalar multiple of the same mode shape; neighbouring regions may move in opposite directions. Normal modes of a double pendulum show that normal modes also describe coupled discrete systems, beyond strings. Their shapes are eigenvectors, rather than spatial eigenfunctions. [ref]
For the ideal wave equation on a string, take a uniform string of length L with constant tension τ and linear mass density μ. Assume small transverse slope, negligible bending stiffness, no damping, and fixed endpoints. Its wave speed is c=τ/μ​, and the nonzero normal modes are
un​(x,t)=Asin(Lnπx​)cos(ωn​t+φ),ωn​=Lnπc​,fn​=2πωn​​=2Lnc​,n=1,2,3,….
(38)
The angular frequency ωn​ is in radians per second; the frequency fn​ is in hertz. The wavelength is 2L/n. The mode shape has n loops separated by nodes of a standing wave, including both fixed endpoints. [ref]
As a worked example, choose L=1m, τ=1N, and μ=1kgm−1. Then c=1ms−1 and f1​=0.5Hz, f2​=1Hz, f3​=1.5Hz. Their oscillation periods are T1​=2s, T2​=1s, and T3​=2/3s. These are deliberately simple model parameters, rather than measurements of a musical instrument. The plot divides displacement by A so that the three mode shapes can be compared, and uses each mode's own oscillation period for its snapshots.
For φ=0, at t=Tn​/4 every point has zero displacement, but most points have nonzero velocity. Only zeros of the mode shape are permanent nodes of a standing wave. At t=Tn​/2 the original mode shape has reversed sign, and at t=Tn​ it returns. The synchronized conversion between kinetic energy and potential energy is shown in normal-mode energy exchange.
The short derivation uses separation of variables: substituting u=ϕq into the wave equation gives ϕ′′+k2ϕ=0 and q′′+c2k2q=0. The fixed-end boundary conditions remove the cosine spatial term and require sin(kL)=0, hence k=nπ/L and ωn​=ck. Different geometries and boundary conditions give different eigenfunctions; a sine mode shape is a property of this uniform fixed string, not a universal form of an eigenmode.
The usefulness is that a complicated vibration becomes a collection of harmonic oscillators. For sufficiently regular fixed-end initial data, the Fourier sine series gives
u(x,t)=∑n=1∞​sin(Lnπx​)[an​cos(ωn​t)+bn​sin(ωn​t)].
(39)
The initial displacement and velocity determine an​ and bn​. This is the superposition principle in a Fourier sine basis, and modal energy distribution measures how strongly each normal mode is excited. The striking simplification is that each component keeps its identity while their sum can continually change shape. [ref]
These independent normal modes belong to the linear model. At larger slopes, changing tension introduces nonlinear effects and can couple the modes. A linearly damped string still admits a Fourier sine basis, but its temporal factors decay and need not oscillate; its energy dissipation identity for a linearly damped string replaces conservation of energy. More general damping need not leave undamped mode shapes independent.

Distinct squared traction-free eigenfrequencies in a bounded lossless elastic body have eigenfunctions orthogonal in L2(D,ρdV)3, by the Betti identity for elastodynamic fields. This is an orthonormal set in a separable Hilbert space, so it is countable: disjoint balls of radius less than 1/2​ around its unit vectors must contain distinct points of a countable dense set. Positive and negative frequency partners add at most a factor of two. This argument proves countability without requiring a separate compact-resolvent proof.

Historically, d'Alembert studied the vibrating-string problem in “Recherches sur la courbe que forme une corde tendue mise en vibration”, in the Berlin Academy's volume for the year 1747, pages 214–219. A wavenumber measures how rapidly a wave phase changes with distance. Two conventions coexist: angular wavenumber counts radians per unit length, while ordinary spatial frequency counts cycles per unit length. For a monochromatic wave with wavelength λ>0,
K=λ2π​,νx​=λ1​,K=2πνx​.
(51)
Here K≥0 is the magnitude of the angular wavenumber. The symbol k can instead denote a signed one-dimensional angular wavenumber: a factor eikx has wavelength 2π/∣k∣ for real k=0. Both conventions have dimensions of inverse length; writing radm−1 or “cycles per metre” exposes the convention. A quoted value in m−1 alone does not resolve the factor of 2π. Spectroscopic wavenumber usually uses the cycles-per-length convention.[ref]
For a real monochromatic plane wave, fix the convention
u(x,t)=Acosϕ(x,t),ϕ=k⋅x−ωt+ϕ0​,K=∣k∣.
(52)
The wavevector k supplies both the spatial wave phase slope and the normal to the wavefronts; its dot product with position makes the wave phase constant on parallel planes. The angular frequency is ω=2πf, with f>0 the ordinary frequency. Moving a distance λ along k changes the wave phase by 2π. Holding a wave crest's wave phase fixed gives its phase velocity ωk/K2 and phase speed
vp​=Kω​=fλ.
(53)
In one dimension the signed phase velocity is ω/k. This identifies a moving pattern; it does not identify the motion of the medium's particles or a wave packet's group velocity.

Wavelength (λ)

Words: 939 Articles: 4
Wavenumber OurBigBook.com
The wavelength λ is the spatial period of a monochromatic wave, measured at a fixed time along the wavevector. For a plane wave with a sinusoid as its profile, it is the distance between consecutive wave crests, or between any consecutive points with the same wave phase modulo 2π:
λ=∣k∣2π​=fvp​​.
(56)
Here k uses angular wavenumber, f is ordinary frequency, and vp​ is phase speed. A distance between arbitrary zero crossings need not be a wavelength: consecutive zeros of a sinusoid are only λ/2 apart, with opposite slopes. In a standing wave, consecutive nodes of a standing wave are also λ/2 apart; λ refers to the constituent travelling waves, even though the nodes of a standing wave do not travel.
Across a stationary interface between stationary linear media, the incident, reflected and transmitted monochromatic waves have the same frequency. The boundary conditions must hold at every time: terms oscillating with different angular frequencies cannot cancel throughout the entire time record. Each medium's dispersion relation then determines its own angular wavenumber and wavelength, so
f1​=f2​,λ1​λ2​​=vp,1​vp,2​​.
(57)
For electromagnetic radiation in a transparent medium with refractive index n, vp​=c0​/n and λ=λ0​/n, where c0​ is the vacuum speed of light. A synthetic example with λ0​=600nm and n=1.5 gives λ=400nm at the same frequency. This conservation argument assumes time-independent linear material response and a stationary interface in the chosen frame. A moving interface can produce a Doppler effect; time-dependent or nonlinear response can change or generate frequencies.[ref]
A broad frequency spectrum generally supplies many component wavelengths, rather than one wavelength for an entire pulse. Even two tones have both their individual wavelengths and a different overall repetition distance: the 2- and 8-cycle-per-metre sum in spatial sampling of a wave repeats after 0.50m, but contains the finer 0.125m structure. A narrow wave packet can have an approximate carrier wavelength; the wave envelope propagates approximately at group velocity, determined by the slope of the dispersion relation. Substituting that group velocity into λ=vp​/f generally gives the wrong carrier wavelength. Where the medium varies slowly, local wavelength gives a more useful description.

Acoustic wavelength measurement (λ=2d)

Words: 510 Articles: 2
Wavelength OurBigBook.com
An acoustic wavelength measurement makes an invisible spatial pattern readable with a ruler. The authored guide Interesting and inexpensive experiments for high school physics by Joe Wolfe places a loudspeaker near a pipe's open end, drives it with an oscillator, and slides a microphone attached to a metre rule through the pipe. An oscilloscope or computer displays the microphone signal. Its oscillation amplitude rises and falls with position; adjacent minima locate pressure nodes of a standing wave a distance d=λ/2 apart. A cap gives a pressure antinode at the closed end; an open end has a pressure node just outside it. These are pressure patterns, distinct from displacement patterns. The guide advises wavelengths longer than the pipe diameter, sufficient pipe length to locate both a node and an antinode, and frequency spectrum analysis to distinguish the intended tone from other sounds.[ref]
The inference follows from superposition of two oppositely directed acoustic plane waves. In an ideal uniform, lossless pipe, taking equal pressure amplitudes P and a rigid cap at x=0 gives
p′(x,t)=Pcos(kx−ωt)+Pcos(kx+ωt)=2Pcos(kx)cos(ωt).
(58)
The time-varying pressure perturbation p′ has local oscillation amplitude 2∣Pcos(kx)∣. Its zeros are separated by π/∣k∣=λ/2. Unequal incident and reflected amplitudes leave nonzero minima, but their spacing remains λ/2 in this ideal model. A microphone detects that pressure variation through a changing electrical signal, rather than watching a wave crest move. Record the tone's frequency too, then infer phase speed vp​=2fd.
For proposed controls, keep the drive frequency and amplitude fixed during a scan, verify the frequency on the recorded signal, and repeat the scan in both directions. Fit several minimum positions xj​=a+jd using linear regression to reduce dependence on one pair of positions. Check the ruler scale and use one consistent reference point on the microphone. Compare with the source switched off to locate background measurement noise; use frequency spectrum analysis to check for additional tones, and reduce drive if the trace ceases to resemble a sinusoid. Record air temperature and avoid strong air motion. These are suggested controls, not additional procedures or observations attributed to the guide.
The pipe must support approximately plane waves over the measured region: transverse structure at shorter wavelengths, the microphone's finite size, and disturbance by the ruler can compromise the interpretation. Weak reflection gives shallow minima, while damping and other reflections can shift the extrema of the simple two-wave model. Measure interior spacings rather than assuming the first minimum is exactly at the pipe lip. A short scan may not include enough minima to estimate d reliably, and drift during sequential scanning can imitate spatial variation.
For an explicitly hypothetical calculation, f=1000Hz and d=0.1715m give λ=0.3430m, K≃18.3183radm−1, and vp​=343.0ms−1. No such measurements are claimed here. If independent small measurement errors in f and fitted d have standard deviations σf​ and σd​, first-order error propagation gives σvp​​/vp​≃(σf​/f)2+(σd​/d)2​. A systematic scale error or changing air conditions requires separate assessment.

Dispersion relation (ω(k))

Words: 5k Articles: 50
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
A dispersion relation specifies which angular frequencies and wavevectors a linear wave model admits. Fix the plane wave convention
u(x,t)=Re{aei(k⋅x−ωt)},D(ω,k)=0.
(59)
Here a is a constant complex amplitude, k is the wavevector, and ω is the angular frequency. Substitution into a constant-coefficient linear partial differential equation replaces ∂t​ by −iω and ∇ by ik, turning the wave problem into an algebraic condition. A system can have several roots; ω=ω(k) means one chosen branch, rather than a promise that the full dispersion relation is single-valued. For real k, Imω>0 means temporal growth in this convention, while Imω<0 means damping. The real-branch discussion of phase velocity and group velocity below assumes negligible loss.
For the one-dimensional wave equation utt​=c2uxx​, the dispersion relation is ω2=c2k2. The branch ω=ck carries right-moving travelling waves for c>0; both its phase velocity and group velocity are c. One may instead use the positive-angular frequency branch ω=c∣k∣, with right-moving components at k>0 and left-moving components at k<0. A real wave pairs each (k,ω) with (−k,−ω); that conjugate pair represents the same travelling pattern. Branch and sign choices therefore matter when interpreting a dispersion diagram.
A particularly tangible dispersive example is a small-amplitude surface gravity wave on still water of uniform depth h. Neglect surface tension and viscosity, assume incompressible flow and irrotational flow, and impose a flat impermeable bottom. With k>0 and positive angular frequency,
ω2=gktanh(kh),g>0.
(60)
Here g is gravitational acceleration and tanh is the hyperbolic tangent. Deep water means kh≫1: ω≃gk​ and longer wavelengths have larger phase speed. Shallow water means kh≪1: ω≃gh​k, an approximately nondispersive wave. Thus depth relative to wavelength, rather than depth alone, determines whether crests and wave packets travel together.[ref]
The dispersion diagram below also includes the ideal deep-water capillary wave limit ω=γ/ρ​k3/2, where γ is surface tension and ρ is mass density. This limit requires the surface tension restoring term to dominate gravity; it reverses the trend of the surface gravity wave, giving larger phase speed at shorter wavelength. The combined gravity-capillary wave has ω2=gk+(γ/ρ)k3.[ref]
The curves use dimensionless normalizations chosen separately for each model; they are analytical diagrams, not experimental data. Their beauty is that a single dispersion relation encodes several observable behaviours: its value gives the angular frequency, its origin-to-point slope gives the one-dimensional phase velocity, its tangent slope gives the group velocity, and variation of that tangent slope predicts distortion of a wave packet. A straight line through the origin describes a nondispersive wave; an affine branch ω=ck+b with b=0 has constant group velocity but phase velocity c+b/k, so those properties must be distinguished.

Choosing ω>0 makes positive k mean rightward phase velocity and negative k mean leftward phase velocity. Reversing both signs leaves the real plane wave and its phase velocity unchanged. At k=0 there are no spatial crests to track, so ω/k is undefined; a finite limit as k→0 is a limiting phase speed, not the speed of a spatially uniform oscillation.
In several dimensions, a plane wave has wave phase k⋅x−ωt+ϕ0​. Constant-wave phase planes obey k⋅v=ω. Their normal phase velocity is

(69)
Tangential motion within a plane does not move that wavefront, which is why the normal direction fixes the vector convention. In an anisotropic medium the group velocity need not point along this wavevector. Likewise the horizontal phase velocity of a tilted wavefront is its crossing speed along a horizontal line, rather than a component of the normal phase velocity.
For the nondispersive wave branch ω=ck, a wave crest and a wave envelope both move at c. For deep-water surface gravity waves, ω=gk​ gives cp​=g/k​ and group velocity cg​=cp​/2. With the illustrative choices g=9.81ms−2 and λ=1m, the model predicts cp​≃1.25ms−1 and cg​≃0.625ms−1. These are calculated values for negligible surface tension and sufficiently large kh, not measurements. A wave crest moves forward through the wave packet, so timing a crest does not time the packet's journey.
There is a direct laboratory meaning to this distinction. MIT's 2005 surface-wave lab uses a long water tank, a controllable hydraulic paddle, and an absorbing beach. Resistance probes convert submerged length into voltage; calibration converts their readouts into free surface elevation versus time. Two probes a known distance apart, backed by a ruler and stopwatch, let students time a wave crest and separately time a feature of the wave packet. The lab records depth and varies frequency and wave amplitude.[ref]
For a clean measurement of phase velocity, fit the periodic portion of both records or follow one identifiable wave crest. A phase difference is only known modulo 2π: probe spacing below half the shortest relevant wavelength, or continuity while sweeping frequency, avoids assigning the wrong whole-cycle delay. Then compare the timed phase velocity with λ/T. Tracking pepper grains instead measures fluid-particle motion, which has a different meaning from either phase velocity or group velocity.
The Klein-Gordon packet velocities example makes the distinction especially sharp: its phase velocity exceeds c, yet its narrow wave envelope moves below c. A carrier wave labels successive oscillations; its speed alone does not establish information velocity. The front velocity depends on the full causal model, including angular frequencies far outside the carrier's narrow range.

Curvature of the dispersion relation eventually changes the wave envelope.[ref]
Two nearby plane waves make the derivative visible without an integral. For equal wave amplitudes a, define kˉ=(k1​+k2​)/2, ωˉ=(ω1​+ω2​)/2, Δk=k2​−k1​ and Δω=ω2​−ω1​. The superposition principle gives the exact identity
acos(k1​x−ω1​t)+acos(k2​x−ω2​t)=2acos(2Δkx−Δωt​)cos(kˉx−ωˉt).
(73)
The periodic wave envelope has speed Δω/Δk, approaching group velocity as the two wavenumbers coalesce, while the carrier wave phase has speed ωˉ/kˉ. Two tones alone form an infinite beat train, not a localized wave packet. The figure shows an exact two-tone surface gravity wave model with dimensionless ω=k​: k1​=0.9, k2​=1.1. Its carrier phase velocity is approximately 0.99875, its finite-difference envelope velocity approximately 0.50063, and ω′(1)=0.5 is the limiting group velocity. The marked carrier phase line need not coincide exactly with a maximum of the full modulated wave.
The deep-water surface gravity wave therefore has cg​=cp​/2, whereas the deep-water capillary wave limit has cg​=3cp​/2: crests can drift either forward or backward relative to a wave envelope. For finite-depth surface gravity waves, differentiating the dispersion relation gives
cg​=2cp​​(1+sinh(2kh)2kh​),k>0.
(74)
Here sinh is the hyperbolic sine. The shallow-water limit has cg​≃cp​≃gh​; the deep-water limit has cg​≃cp​/2.[ref]
In the wave tank, produce a finite train with a smooth turn-on and turn-off and time the same wave envelope feature at two probes separated by distance L; its transit estimate is L/Δt. Independently follow wave crests through that train. Techet's 2003 lab asks students to observe a deep-water train's foremost crest disappearing as the group moves forward, and to compare deep- and shallow-water cases. The interpretation is that a wave crest overtakes the slower wave envelope, dwindling at its front while other crests become visible at its rear. This is a qualitative expected observation in the teaching protocol, not a published set of measured curves.[ref]
A useful controlled version keeps the paddle wave amplitude small, records h and λ, and checks both ka≪1 and a/h≪1. Compare runs with kh≫1 and kh≪1, rather than assuming every ripple tank is shallow relative to every wavelength. Increase train duration at fixed central frequency to narrow its spectrum, and check that the envelope transit estimate stabilizes. Calibrate both probes, sample fast enough to resolve the carrier, and compare records before reflected waves return; an absorbing beach reduces this contamination. A current changes laboratory velocities, large wave amplitudes introduce nonlinear effects, and very short wavelengths require surface tension. Strong damping or noticeable reshaping makes the chosen threshold or peak an unreliable marker of simple group velocity. These are proposed controls and model limits, not claims that the cited lab measured every correction.
Three velocities should consequently be kept separate. The group velocity predicts narrow-band wave envelope motion. An energy-transport velocity is energy flux divided by energy density, using the appropriate time average; it agrees with group velocity in standard lossless linear wave models when all stored energy is included.[ref] A signal-front velocity concerns the earliest response to a new disturbance and requires a causal model over its full spectrum. A strictly band-limited wave packet has no sharply bounded onset, and a mathematical two-tone envelope cannot test front arrival. In strongly absorbing or broadband propagation, a single group velocity need not describe the observed peak, energy transport, or first detectable response. A complex ω or k also prevents interpreting its derivative as an ordinary real transport velocity without further analysis.
In particular, an unusually large or negative group velocity from pulse reshaping does not establish superluminal information transmission. For the causal dielectric model analysed by Fitzpatrick, the field ahead of the front vanishes for t<x/c, even when its phase velocity exceeds the vacuum speed of light c. That result concerns the electromagnetic model's causality; the ideal water-wave diagrams above contain no relativistic signal-front claim.[ref]
Finally, zero wavenumber requires care: the positive-frequency wave equation branch c∣k∣ is not differentiable at k=0, so it has no unique group velocity there, although its one-sided values are ±c. A smooth gapped branch such as the Klein-Gordon equation instead has ω′(0)=0 despite undefined phase velocity at k=0. The same signed branch must be used in both derivatives and ratios; a negative group velocity means an envelope moving in the negative coordinate direction, not a negative elapsed time. The practical value of group velocity is precisely this translation between a local slope on a dispersion diagram and a measurable packet transit, with its assumptions made explicit.
The Gaussian envelope in a Klein-Gordon medium supplies a quantitative next step: the first derivative translates the wave envelope, the second derivative spreads it, and higher derivatives limit that approximation. At finite spectral width, a peak's measured speed need not equal the group velocity at the central wavenumber. Neither a peak nor a fixed fraction of its height generally identifies front velocity.

Front velocity (vf​)

Words: 401
Phase velocity and group velocity OurBigBook.com
The front velocity is the propagation speed of the earliest boundary of a newly introduced disturbance's support. It asks when an initially unaffected observer can first respond, whereas group velocity asks how a narrow wave envelope translates. A detector threshold defines a practical arrival time, but can miss arbitrarily small earlier responses; a packet peak is another distinct timing convention. In a causal dielectric model, a high-angular frequency contour argument gives exactly zero field for t<x/c, even when phase velocity exceeds c. This is a statement about that model's relativistic causality, not a universal identification of group velocity with front velocity.[ref]
For the stipulated Klein-Gordon equation with compactly supported real Cauchy data, front velocity is bounded by c, and c is the model's maximal speed of influence. A short energy method outline uses
e=21​(ut2​+c2ux2​+ω02​u2),J=−c2ut​ux​,∂t​e+∂x​J=0,∣J∣≤ce.
(75)
Integration outside an expanding interval shows that zero initial energy there remains zero. Thus initial support in [−a,a] cannot influence x>a before t=(x−a)/c. The positive energy density includes the restoring term ω02​u2/2: this adds oscillation behind the front without extending its domain of dependence. A particular disturbance may fail to excite the leading boundary, so the maximal speed is not a promise of a detectable response for every source.
A Gaussian function is nonzero arbitrarily far away, so the Gaussian envelope in a Klein-Gordon medium has no sharp initial support boundary. Its small distant tails are already in the initial data. Likewise, keeping only a narrow interval of the frequency spectrum cannot reproduce an exact abrupt onset. Cutting off a Gaussian tail changes its Fourier transform and the accompanying initial velocity; it is a different initial-value problem. The exponential initial-velocity tail for the Klein-Gordon equation is another concrete example of a pre-existing tail outside the main disturbance.
The water-tank measurement in phase velocity records free surface elevation with calibrated resistance probes and uses a ruler and stopwatch for an independent check. The inspected protocol calls the front or back of a group a timing feature. That visible edge establishes an envelope transit estimate, not the first nonzero disturbance in the sense of front velocity.[ref] A proposed additional control would repeat the transit fit at several detection thresholds and train durations, using matched probe calibration and the same sampling rate. Dependence on the threshold diagnoses wave envelope reshaping or limited sensitivity; records should be compared before reflections return. Such a test could expose limitations of a group velocity estimate, but would not establish an exact causal front or validate the stipulated Klein-Gordon equation for water waves.

Information velocity

Words: 100
Phase velocity and group velocity OurBigBook.com
An information velocity must specify what counts as a newly distinguishable message and how it is detected. In a causal model, receivers cannot distinguish two otherwise identical preparations before their difference can arrive. Front velocity therefore bounds the arrival of genuinely new changes when the model has a finite domain of dependence. Group velocity can estimate the delay of a weakly distorted narrow wave packet, but it is not a universal speed of information: damping, amplification and reshaping can move the peak without advancing the first possible response. A Gaussian peak shift alone does not test relativistic causality.[ref]

Crest and trough

Words: 45 Articles: 2
Phase velocity and group velocity OurBigBook.com
The wave crest and wave trough are respectively the highest and lowest displacements in a wave.
Wave crest
Words: 24
Crest and trough OurBigBook.com
A wave crest is a local maximum of the wave's displacement. In a monochromatic travelling wave it lies at a fixed phase and propagates at the phase velocity.
Wave trough
Words: 9
Crest and trough OurBigBook.com
A wave trough is a local minimum of the wave's displacement.

Wave packet

Words: 560 Articles: 3
Phase velocity and group velocity OurBigBook.com
A wave packet is a localized superposition of Fourier modes. In a narrow packet, nearby wavenumbers interfere to produce a slowly varying wave envelope around a rapid carrier wave. Its leading translation is governed by group velocity; the carrier's wave phase follows phase velocity. Localized does not necessarily mean compact support: a Gaussian function decays rapidly but extends over the whole line. The Gaussian envelope in a Klein-Gordon medium gives an original example with both translation and spreading.
Envelope (waves)
Words: 83
Wave packet OurBigBook.com
A wave envelope is a slowly varying wave amplitude multiplying a rapidly oscillating carrier wave. For a complex wavefield ψ=A(x,t)ei(k0​x−ωc​t), its nonnegative amplitude envelope is ∣A∣=∣ψ∣; the complex A can also encode a slowly varying wave phase. This choice distinguishes the amplitude envelope from a signed modulation factor, such as the cosine factor in a two-tone superposition. A slowly varying wave envelope is useful when the carrier's wavelength and period are short compared with its variation scales. Strong overlap between distinct packets or a broad frequency spectrum can spoil a unique carrier-envelope interpretation.
Carrier wave (ei(k0​x−ωc​t))
Words: 63
Wave packet OurBigBook.com
A carrier wave is the rapid reference oscillation in a modulated wave. In the narrow-packet representation ψ=A(x,t)ei(k0​x−ωc​t), choose k0​ near the centre of the frequency spectrum and ωc​=ω(k0​) on its dispersion relation. Its constant-wave phase reference moves at phase velocity ωc​/k0​. This reference need not coincide with a local maximum of the complete real wavefield when the wave envelope varies. Moving the reference k0​ shifts some slow wave phase into A without changing ψ.
Gaussian envelope in a Klein-Gordon medium (L(t)=σ−11+β2t2σ4​)
Words: 357
Wave packet OurBigBook.com
For the stipulated Klein-Gordon packet velocities, take the original normalized spectral amplitude
a(k)=2π​σ1​exp[−2σ2(k−k0​)2​],ψ(x,t)=∫R​a(k)ei[kx−ω(k)t]dk,
(76)
with k0​>0 and 0<σ≪k0​. Here σ is the width of the spectral amplitude, not the standard deviation of its squared magnitude. Initially ψ(x,0)=e−σ2x2/2eik0​x, a Gaussian function multiplying a carrier wave. Taking u=Reψ gives a real solution of the Klein-Gordon equation with the corresponding initial velocity. The tiny negative-k tail is retained in this exact integral; the statement that it is mainly right-going is a narrow-spectrum approximation, not a claim of strictly positive wavenumbers.
The dimensionless figure uses c=ω0​=k0​=1 and σ=0.18 at t=0,4,8. Blue curves are Reψ, orange bounds are ±∣ψ∣, and the marked carrier wave reference is x=vp​t; it need not be a crest of the full wavefield. The dashed envelope-centre reference x=vg​t is a leading approximation. These are calculated curves, not experimental records. The exact dispersion relation makes the packet slightly asymmetric; a quadratic approximation predicts symmetric broadening about vg​t.
The first-order Taylor expansion translates the initial wave envelope without changing its shape. Retaining curvature instead gives
ω(k)≃ωc​+vg​q+21​βq2,q=k−k0​,β=ω′′(k0​)=ωc3​c2ω02​​>0.
(77)
The distinction between translation and curvature-driven spreading is the same one exposed by the Gaussian pulse calculation in Pulse Propagation by Richard Fitzpatrick (equations 9.8–9.18). Its first-order approximation is not an assertion that a dispersive packet keeps its shape indefinitely.
Evaluating the quadratic Gaussian integral gives the original approximation
ψ2​(x,t)=1+iβtσ2​ei(k0​x−ωc​t)​exp[−2(1+iβtσ2)σ2(x−vg​t)2​],
(78)
and hence
∣ψ2​(x,t)∣=(1+β2t2σ4)−1/4exp[−2L(t)2(x−vg​t)2​],L(t)=σ1+β2t2σ4​​.
(79)
Here L is the amplitude width: the standard deviation of the normalized intensity ∣ψ2​∣2 is L/2​. The peak falls as the packet widens, while ∫∣ψ2​∣2dx stays constant. This conserved integral is not the complete physical wave energy of the Klein-Gordon equation.
Rigid translation requires ∣β∣tσ2≪1. The quadratic approximation can allow that quantity to be order one, but still requires the accumulated neglected cubic wave phase to be small over the appreciable spectrum, for example (t/6)sup∣q∣≤3σ​∣ω′′′(k0​+q)∣(3σ)3≪1. This sufficient check controls only the stated three-width spectral window; the Gaussian tails must also be negligible at the required accuracy. Higher derivatives or very long times require returning to the exact spectral integral. The width L(t) is therefore a controlled local approximation; it neither predicts front velocity nor establishes a universal identity between group velocity and information velocity.

Klein-Gordon equation

Wave equation OurBigBook.com
The one-dimensional Klein-Gordon equation
ϕtt​−c2ϕxx​+A2c2ϕ=0
(81)
has positive-frequency dispersion relation ω(k)=ck2+A2​.

Exponential initial-velocity tail for the Klein-Gordon equation (u(x,t)=te−∣x∣(∣x∣>t))

Words: 63
Klein-Gordon equation OurBigBook.com
For utt​=uxx​−u with u(x,0)=0 and ut​(x,0)=e−∣x∣, the solution outside ∣x∣≤t is exactly te−∣x∣. On the positive half-line, te−x satisfies both the equation and initial data; the finite propagation speed limits dependence at x>t to positive initial points. Uniqueness on this domain of dependence proves the formula there, and reflection gives the negative half-line. The exterior tail is nonzero because the initial velocity is not compactly supported.

Stationary-phase asymptotic of a Klein-Gordon wave along a subluminal ray

Words: 62 Articles: 1
Klein-Gordon equation OurBigBook.com
For zero initial velocity and Fourier amplitude a(k), observation along x=Vt with 0≤V<c selects the two stationary wavenumbers ±k0​, where
k0​=c2−V2​AV​.
(82)
Writing s=c2−V2​, the leading oscillation has angular frequency As and amplitude proportional to t−1/2.

Upward zero crossings of an oscillatory stationary-phase tail

Ωt+γ=23π​+2πn
(83)
